implementation_notes: Do not hand-roll this in Java either. java.util.concurrent supplies ConcurrentLinkedQueue (lock-free, based on Michael and Scott), ConcurrentHashMap (lock-free reads, CAS-based bin updates), ConcurrentLinkedDeque, and the AtomicInteger family; all are audited implementations. Java adds two things worth knowing: the intrinsics (compareAndSet, compareAndSwap) are the CAS the algorithms build on and are what the collections use, and jdk.internal Unsafe / VarHandle give the memory ordering. Beyond that, the JVM's own GC pauses mean the tail latency is dominated by collection, so a hand-rolled lock-free structure rarely improves the observable tail. Virtual threads change the calculus only for blocking work, not for CPU contention.
idiom_name: java.util.concurrent lock-free collections (ConcurrentLinkedQueue, ConcurrentHashMap) over AtomicInteger.compareAndSet
pitfalls: AtomicInteger on a single cache line is the wrong answer for a contended counter - LongAdder's striping exists precisely because of this.
ConcurrentHashMap's lock-free guarantee is about its internal updates; compound operations on it (check-then-act across get and put) are not atomic without compute() or merge().
Blocking inside a compute() on a ConcurrentHashMap can deadlock or exceed the bin's lock - the lambda must not touch the map again.
The GC pauses dominate tail latency, so a hand-tuned lock-free counter rarely moves the number users observe; measure the tail before optimising it.
alternative: ConcurrentHashMap and the java.util.concurrent collections; java.util.concurrent.locks for explicit locking; BlockingQueue for producer-consumer
